extracted.intended_audience: researchers in science communication, university press officers, science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing exaggeration in health-related academic press releases (and resultant news) by comparing press releases and news stories to their associated peer-reviewed articles, using categories of advice, causal claims, and human inference from non-human studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration — advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration in advice: press releases or news that contain stronger or additional advice compared to the associated peer-reviewed article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by comparing press releases and news to their associated peer-reviewed articles to identify when advice is stronger or newly introduced in the PR/news than in the article. The study reports rates and comparisons (figures show percentages and 95% CIs) and notes that the association between news and press releases did not replicate for advice exaggeration in this cohort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration — causal claims from correlational evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration when a press release or news item presents causal claims despite the underlying peer-reviewed study providing only correlational evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised by comparing the strength of causal language in PR/news with that in the peer-reviewed article. The replication study found the association between news and press releases did replicate for causal-claim exaggeration. Use categorical coding (causal vs correlational) and report percentages with confidence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration — human inference from non-human studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration when press releases or news infer effects in humans from studies conducted on non-human samples (e.g., animal studies) beyond what the original article supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified by checking whether PR/news make human-directed claims or implications not present in the original non-human study. The study observed lower base exaggeration rates for this category, possibly reflecting policies such as the UK Concordat on Openness on Animal Research. Report prevalence and compare PR vs news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison-to-source standard (method for defining exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is defined by direct comparison of press releases and news items to the associated peer-reviewed articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The methodological standard used: pair each press release and news story with the peer-reviewed article it reports on and code differences in advice, causal language, and human inference. Results are summarised as percentages (with 95% CIs) of PRs/news that contain exaggeration relative to the article. This is the operational rubric for judging whether a PR or news item is exaggerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength alignment between press releases and news
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of statements in news stories is normally associated with the strength of statements in the corresponding press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether stronger statements in a PR correspond to stronger statements in subsequent news coverage; the study reports that news statement strength is typically associated with PR statement strength, implying press releases are influential on how strongly findings are reported in the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake relative to exaggeration (coverage incentive test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether exaggerated press releases attract more news coverage (news uptake) compared to non-exaggerated press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found no evidence that exaggerated press releases attract significantly more news. As an evaluative criterion, this suggests that exaggeration should not be justified as an effective strategy for increasing press coverage. Measure by comparing rates of news pickup for exaggerated vs non-exaggerated PRs and report differences with confidence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reporting metric (prevalence and confidence intervals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report exaggeration prevalence as percentages with 95% confidence intervals when comparing press releases and news to journal articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures in the paper present percentage of press releases/news containing exaggeration (by category) with 95% CIs; use similar summary statistics when evaluating PRs. Useful for replication and comparison with prior studies (e.g., Sumner et al. 2014).
